statement: 2009 points have been marked on a circle. Lucía colors them with 7 different colors of her choice. Then Iván can join three points of the same color, forming monochrome triangles. Triangles cannot have points in common — not even vertices in common. Iván's goal is to draw as many monochrome triangles as possible; Lucía's objective is to prevent Iván's task as much as possible through a good choice of coloring. How many monochrome triangles will Iván get if they both do their homework to the best of their ability?

A positive integer \(n\) is acceptable if the sum of the squares of its proper divisors equals \(2n + 4\). (A divisor of \(n\) is proper if it is different from 1 and from \(n\).) Find all acceptable numbers less than \(10000\).

Isosceles trapezoid \(ABCD\), with \(AB \parallel CD\), is such that there exists a circle \(\Gamma\) tangent to its four sides. Let \(T = \Gamma \cap BC\) and \(P = \Gamma \cap AT\) (\(P \neq T\)). If \(\dfrac{AP}{AT} = \dfrac{2}{5}\), compute \(\dfrac{AB}{CD}\).

You have 100 equal rods. It is allowed to split each rod into two or three shorter rods (not necessarily equal). The objective is that by rearranging all pieces, \(q > 200\) new rods of equal length can be assembled. Find all values of \(q\) for which this can be done.

Around a circle are written 2009 integers (not necessarily distinct) such that the difference between any two neighboring numbers is 1 or 2. A number is huge if it is greater than both its neighbors, and tiny if it is less than both its neighbors. The sum of all the huge numbers equals the sum of all the tiny numbers plus 1810. Determine how many odd numbers there can be around the circumference.

A sequence \(a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, \ldots\) is such that \(a_0 = 1\) and, for each \(n \geq 0\), \(a_{n+1} = m \cdot a_n\), where \(m\) is an integer between 2 and 9 inclusive. Also, every integer between 2 and 9 has been used at least once to obtain \(a_{n+1}\) from \(a_n\). Let \(S_n\) be the sum of the digits of \(a_n\), for \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\). Prove that \(S_n \geq S_{n+1}\) for infinitely many values of \(n\).
